key_terms.meaning: An executing program with its own resources such as memory, registers and open files.
The status of a process: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, or Terminated.
Process Control Block; a data structure that holds a process's state, registers, memory limits and accounting information.
Saving the PCB of the running process and loading the PCB of the next process to run.
A queue that holds all processes in the Ready state waiting for CPU time.
System call (e.g., fork) that allocates a new PCB and copies the parent’s resources.
System call (e.g., exit) that releases a process’s resources and removes its PCB.
IPC method where two or more processes map the same physical memory region.
IPC method that uses send/receive primitives to exchange data without shared address space.
Unidirectional byte stream used for communication between related processes.
A lightweight execution unit that shares the address space of its parent process.
Mapping of user threads to kernel threads: many‑to‑one, one‑to‑one, many‑to‑many.
Quantitative measure such as CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, or response time.
Scheduler may interrupt a running process to give CPU to a higher‑priority one.
First‑Come‑First‑Served; schedules processes in order of arrival without preemption.
Completely Fair Scheduler; Linux’s modern scheduler that assigns virtual runtime to each task.

takeaways: A process is the OS abstraction for a running program and is described by its PCB.
Context switching moves the CPU from one process to another by saving and restoring PCBs.
Threads share the same address space, making communication cheap but requiring synchronization.
Scheduling criteria guide the choice of algorithm based on system goals such as high utilization or low response time.
Preemptive algorithms can improve responsiveness but add overhead from more context switches.
Linux uses O(1) and CFS schedulers to balance constant‑time selection with fairness on multicore CPUs.
IPC mechanisms differ in speed, complexity, and suitability for different application patterns.
bank_note: Syllabi stress clear definitions, step‑by‑step OS actions and justification of choices when answering long‑answer questions.

bank.q: Define the Process Control Block (PCB) and list its main components.
outline: Definition of PCB
List of components such as process state, program counter, registers, memory limits, open files

bank.q: Explain the life‑cycle of a process using the standard state diagram.
outline: Describe each state (New, Ready, Running, Waiting, Terminated)
Show transitions caused by events like admit, dispatch, I/O request, exit

bank.q: Given processes P1(Arr=0,Burst=5), P2(Arr=2,Burst=3), P3(Arr=4,Burst=1), schedule them using FCFS and compute the average waiting time.
outline: Order of execution based on arrival
Compute start and finish times for each process
Calculate waiting time for each and average

bank.q: Show the sequence of operations performed by the OS during a context switch from Process A to Process B.
outline: Save registers of A into its PCB
Update A’s state to Ready or Waiting
Load registers of B from its PCB
Update B’s state to Running

bank.q: Compare preemptive and non‑preemptive scheduling in terms of CPU utilization and response time. Use examples to illustrate differences.
outline: Define both types
Explain how preemption can reduce waiting for high‑priority jobs
Show possible increase in context‑switch overhead
Provide example scenarios

bank.q: Critically evaluate Linux’s Completely Fair Scheduler against the older O(1) scheduler for a multi‑core web server workload.
outline: Brief description of O(1) and CFS
Discuss fairness, load balancing, latency, and scalability
Explain impact on request latency in a web server
Conclude which is more suitable and why

bank.q: Describe three inter‑process communication mechanisms and give a typical use case for each.
outline: Shared memory – high‑speed data exchange, e.g., video processing
Message passing – client‑server request/reply, e.g., web server
Pipe – linear data flow between parent and child, e.g., shell pipelines

bank.q: Design a threading model for a smartphone chat application. Choose many‑to‑one or many‑to‑many and justify your choice.
outline: Identify tasks (UI, network, encryption)
Map tasks to threads
Explain why many‑to‑many gives better concurrency on multicore phones
Mention synchronization needs

bank.q: Discuss how the choice of scheduling criteria influences algorithm selection in a real‑time embedded system.
outline: List real‑time criteria: deadline miss ratio, jitter
Show why algorithms like Rate‑Monotonic are preferred
Contrast with criteria for general‑purpose systems
Provide example of an automotive control loop

bank.q: List the common scheduling criteria and give a one‑sentence definition for each.
outline: CPU utilization – keep CPU busy
Throughput – number of processes completed per unit time
Turnaround time – total time from submission to completion
Waiting time – time spent in ready queue
Response time – time from request to first response

bank.q: Simulate a Round Robin schedule with time quantum 4 ms for processes P1(6 ms), P2(8 ms), P3(7 ms). Compute each process’s turnaround time.
outline: Create Gantt chart with 4 ms slices
Track remaining burst for each process
Calculate finish time for each and subtract arrival time
Present turnaround times

bank.q: Explain how shared‑memory IPC can lead to race conditions and describe two synchronization techniques to prevent them.
outline: Define race condition
Show example of two processes writing to same location
Introduce mutex lock and semaphore as solutions
Explain how they enforce mutual exclusion

bank.q: Outline the steps performed by the OS during process creation (fork) and program execution (exec).
outline: fork: allocate PCB, copy parent’s address space, set return values
exec: replace address space with new program, reset registers, keep PID
Resulting process runs new program

glossary.def: An executing instance of a program with its own resources.
Current condition of a process: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, or Terminated.
Process Control Block; stores all information needed to manage a process.
The act of saving the state of one process and restoring the state of another.
Queue that holds all processes ready to use the CPU.
OS operation that allocates a new PCB and sets up initial resources.
OS operation that releases all resources of a finished process.
System call that creates a child process by duplicating the parent.
System call that replaces a process’s memory image with a new program.
IPC technique where multiple processes map the same physical memory region.
IPC technique that uses send/receive primitives to exchange data.
Unidirectional byte stream used for communication between related processes.
Lightweight execution unit that shares the parent process’s address space.
Mapping strategy between user threads and kernel threads.
Multiple user threads mapped to a single kernel thread.
Quantitative measure used to evaluate scheduling performance.
Percentage of time the CPU is actively executing processes.
Number of processes completed per unit of time.
Total time from process submission to its completion.
Total time a process spends in the Ready queue.
Scheduler can interrupt a running process to assign CPU to another.
Preemptive algorithm that gives each ready process a fixed time slice.
Completely Fair Scheduler; Linux’s algorithm that distributes CPU time based on virtual runtime.
